corrections.critique: Strongest feature: O'Connor juxtaposes Old Testament authorization with New Testament obedience to cruel masters, exposing why abolitionist reception and liberatory appropriation cannot establish a consistently anti-slavery canon. Principal limitation: The reply establishes textual moral instability, but does not fully defeat a developmental canonical hierarchy treating permissive rules as historically accommodated constraints subordinated to later emancipatory principles. Live burden: D'Souza must justify that hierarchy without merely appealing to beneficial reception, explaining why divinely presented law permits human ownership and why apostolic instruction demands obedience under cruelty while still warranting coherent moral authority. Locked score: Exceptionally direct diagnostic contact, an explicit hypothetical concession, stable scope, proportionate force, and substantial contrary textual evidence justify the very-strong 93, while the unresolved developmental-reading possibility appropriately prevents a higher assessment.
